fields.definition: A tonal descriptor for a boomy, boxy sound caused by excessive resonance in the low-mid range, roughly 150 to 400 Hz, giving a hollow, enclosed quality as if the sound were made inside a small box or tub.
fields.plain_english: A tubby sound is boomy and boxy, with too much low-middle tone. It sounds a bit like talking inside an empty cardboard box.
fields.purpose_function: It flags a build-up of unwanted low-mid resonance so an engineer knows to cut those frequencies for a clearer, more open tone.
fields.practical_application: An engineer hearing a tubby kick, tom, or vocal will sweep an EQ to find and cut the offending low-mid frequencies, often around 200 to 400 Hz.
common_mistakes: Confusing tubby with warm; warmth is pleasant fullness, while tubby is an unwanted boxy resonance.
Boosting low-mids for body and pushing a source into tubbiness.
Cutting far too wide a band to fix tubbiness and thinning out the whole tone.
scenario_contexts: A kick drum recorded in a small untreated room sounding boxy and tubby.
A vocal on a cheap microphone with a boomy low-mid build-up.
Taming a tom that rings with a hollow, tubby resonance.

fields.definition: A tonal descriptor for a sound that lacks high-frequency clarity and detail, as if a thin cover were placed over it, making it dull, distant, and slightly muffled.
fields.plain_english: A veiled sound is missing its clear, detailed highs. It sounds like music playing behind a thin curtain, a little dull and far away.
fields.purpose_function: It describes a loss of top-end openness and detail so an engineer can judge whether a source needs high-frequency lift or a cleaner signal path.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may call a dull microphone or a covered vocal veiled, then add gentle high-shelf EQ or change mic position to restore clarity.
common_mistakes: Confusing veiled with warm; warm is pleasant, while veiled means a loss of wanted detail.
Boosting highs harshly to lift a veiled sound and adding harshness instead of clarity.
Blaming the source when a dirty pop filter, foam, or off-axis mic is veiling the sound.
scenario_contexts: A vocal that sounds dull and covered through a worn or cheap microphone.
Comparing a clear reference monitor with a veiled one that hides detail.
A guitar tone that loses air and detail after heavy low-pass filtering.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a sound or recording with a strong, appealing mood or atmosphere, often coming from characterful gear, room sound, or slight imperfections rather than clinical accuracy.
fields.plain_english: A vibey sound has a strong mood or feel that pulls you in. It is not perfectly clean, but it has character, like an old photo with a warm, moody look.
fields.purpose_function: It describes emotional character and atmosphere so an engineer can aim for feel and mood, not just technical cleanness.
fields.practical_application: An engineer chasing a vibey take may use vintage gear, room mics, tape, or a looser performance instead of a polished, sterile sound.
common_mistakes: Treating vibey as a fixed EQ setting instead of an overall mood created by many choices.
Adding noise or effects to fake a vibe and burying the actual performance.
Assuming vibey means low quality, when a vibey sound is a deliberate creative choice.
scenario_contexts: Using room mics and tape to give a live band recording a vibey feel.
Choosing an old characterful microphone for a moody vocal.
Keeping a slightly imperfect take because it feels more vibey than a clean one.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a sound with the character of older analog equipment, marked by tube warmth, tape saturation, gentle harmonic coloration, and a slightly reduced, smoothed frequency range.
fields.plain_english: A vintage sound copies the warm, colored tone of old analog gear. It is smooth and a little soft on the edges, like a classic record from decades ago.
fields.purpose_function: It describes desirable old-school coloration so an engineer can recreate the warmth and character of classic analog recordings.
fields.practical_application: An engineer wanting a vintage tone may use tube gear, tape emulation, or classic-style plug-ins to add warmth, saturation, and gentle high-end roll-off.
common_mistakes: Assuming vintage always sounds better, when old-style coloration can hurt clarity in a modern mix.
Confusing vintage with simply dark; vintage adds harmonic character, not only reduced highs.
Stacking many vintage emulations and muddying the mix with too much coloration.
scenario_contexts: Using a tape emulation to give a modern drum bus a vintage feel.
Choosing a classic-style tube compressor for a vintage vocal sound.
Recreating a 1960s tone with reduced bandwidth and gentle saturation.

fields.definition: A tonal descriptor for a full, pleasant sound with strong low-mids and fundamentals and a gentle, unforced top end, standing as the opposite of thin or harsh.
fields.plain_english: A warm sound is full and gentle, strong in the low-middle tones with no harsh highs. It feels cozy and easy on the ears.
fields.purpose_function: It describes pleasing low-mid fullness and smooth highs so an engineer can judge whether a source feels full and comfortable or thin and edgy.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may add warmth by boosting low-mids, rolling off harsh highs, or using tube or tape coloration on a thin, brittle source.
common_mistakes: Confusing warm with muddy; warmth is controlled fullness, while mud is uncontrolled low-mid build-up.
Boosting too much low-mid chasing warmth and losing clarity.
Assuming warm means dull, when a warm sound can still have clear, open highs.
scenario_contexts: Adding low-mid body to a thin vocal to make it warmer.
Choosing a ribbon microphone for a warm horn or guitar tone.
Softening harsh digital highs to give a mix a warmer feel.

fields.definition: A descriptor for a signal that contains audible effect processing, especially reverb or delay, as opposed to a dry, unprocessed signal; a fully wet signal is all effect and none of the original sound.
fields.plain_english: A wet sound has effects like reverb or echo added to it, while a dry sound has none. Wet is like the echo you hear in a big empty hall.
fields.purpose_function: It describes how much effect is in a signal so an engineer can set the balance between the processed and the clean sound.
fields.practical_application: An engineer sets a wet/dry mix control or a reverb send level to decide how much effect sits on a vocal or instrument.
common_mistakes: Confusing wet with loud; wet is the amount of effect, not the level of the channel.
Making a mix too wet so vocals sound distant and lose clarity.
Forgetting that a fully wet effect return should carry only the effect, not the dry signal.
scenario_contexts: Setting the reverb send to make a snare sound wetter.
Balancing wet and dry on a vocal delay so the words stay clear.
Using a fully wet reverb return on an aux channel.

fields.definition: A tonal descriptor for a warm, resonant, slightly hollow midrange character like that of a hollow wooden instrument, giving body without a metallic edge.
fields.plain_english: A woody sound is warm and a little hollow in the middle tones, like tapping on a hollow piece of wood. It has body but no metal-like ring.
fields.purpose_function: It describes a natural wooden resonance so an engineer can judge or aim for the organic tone of instruments like clarinet, marimba, or upright bass.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may call a well-recorded clarinet or kick drum woody, or shape the mids to bring out the natural woody body of an acoustic instrument.
common_mistakes: Confusing woody with boxy; woody is a pleasant natural resonance, while boxy is an unwanted one.
Cutting mids too hard and removing the natural woody character of an acoustic instrument.
Assuming woody means dull, when it still carries clear midrange detail.
scenario_contexts: Describing the warm, hollow tone of a well-recorded clarinet or marimba.
Capturing the woody thud of an upright bass.
Shaping a kick drum for a natural, woody attack instead of a clicky one.

fields.definition: A tonal descriptor for excessive, loose, boomy low-frequency energy that is often undamped and lacking definition, producing a dull thump rather than tight, controlled bass.
fields.plain_english: A woofy sound has too much loose, boomy bass with no tightness. It thumps in a dull way, like a big speaker with the bass turned up too high.
fields.purpose_function: It flags an overblown, poorly controlled low end so an engineer knows to tighten or cut the boomy bass frequencies.
fields.practical_application: An engineer hearing a woofy kick or bass will cut the boomy low frequencies and tighten the low end with EQ or damping.
common_mistakes: Confusing woofy with powerful; woofy bass is loose and dull, not tight and strong.
Boosting sub or bass too much and making a source woofy.
Leaving a woofy low end unchecked, which can overdrive and damage small woofers or subs.
scenario_contexts: A bass guitar with loose, boomy notes that lack definition.
A kick drum that thumps woofily in an untreated room.
Tightening a woofy low end on a club system to protect the subs and improve clarity.

fields.definition: A tonal descriptor for a low end or low-mid range that is loose, thick, and poorly defined, sounding muffled and unclear rather than tight and articulate.
fields.plain_english: A woolly sound has thick, loose low tones with no clear edges. It sounds soft and fuzzy, like listening through a thick wool sweater.
fields.purpose_function: It describes a lack of low-end clarity and definition so an engineer can tighten and clean up a muddy, undefined bottom.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may call a muddy bass or vocal woolly, then cut the low-mid build-up and tighten the low end for clearer definition.
common_mistakes: Confusing woolly with warm; warmth is controlled, while woolly is loose and unclear.
Layering too much low-mid and making a mix woolly and muddy.
Trying to fix woolliness with only a level cut instead of targeted EQ and cleanup.
scenario_contexts: A bass guitar that sounds thick and undefined in a busy mix.
Cleaning up a woolly low-mid build-up on an acoustic guitar.
Tightening a woolly kick and bass so they sit clearly together.
